vignette:
**Patient Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 53-year-old Latin American man who presents for an initial consultation at the urging of his primary care physician. He is a tax consultant, a meticulous man who has spent thirty years navigating the labyrinthine rules of the IRS. He is divorced and lives alone in a quiet suburban apartment. He sits stiffly on the edge of the armchair, his hands clasped in his lap, his eyes scanning the room as if cataloging every exit. He speaks in a low, measured tone, as if he is delivering a carefully prepared report.

He begins his story not with the event itself, but with the morning of it. It was a Tuesday, three years ago. He had driven to a client’s office in a neighboring city, a route he knew by heart. He was stopped at a traffic light, thinking about a deduction for a small business owner, when he saw the flashing lights in his rearview mirror. He remembers the precise feeling of his heart dropping, a cold certainty that something was very wrong.

He did not resist. He pulled over immediately, turned off the engine, placed his hands on the steering wheel as he had seen people do in videos. He remembers the officer’s voice, sharp and demanding. He remembers the officer asking for his license and registration. He remembers reaching for the glove compartment, a slow, deliberate movement. He remembers the officer shouting, the door being yanked open, and the feeling of his arm being twisted behind his back. He remembers the cold pressure of a knee on his spine, the gravel digging into his cheek. He remembers the smell of asphalt and sweat and cheap cologne.

He was held for three hours. He was never told why he was stopped. He was never charged. He was released with a warning for a broken taillight, a crack he had not known was there. He drove home in a daze, the world outside the windshield looking unreal, like a movie set.

In the weeks that followed, Mr. A. stopped driving. He told himself it was temporary, that he was just shaken. He began taking the bus, but the bus stops were full of people, and the crowded aisles made his skin crawl. He started working from home exclusively, a shift his firm reluctantly allowed. His apartment, once a place of quiet order, became a fortress. He installed a deadbolt on his bedroom door. He checks the locks on his windows three times before he can sleep.

The hypervigilance is constant. A sudden car horn on the street makes him flinch, his coffee cup clattering against the saucer. A police siren, even a block away, stops his breath. He has a recurring nightmare: he is in his car, but the steering wheel is gone, and the car is driving itself into a dark, endless tunnel. He wakes up gasping, his sheets soaked in sweat.

His work, once a source of pride, has become a minefield. He can no longer handle audits. The thought of an official letter with a government seal sends a wave of nausea through him. He has taken to avoiding the mail, letting it pile up in a basket by the door. He has lost two major clients because he missed deadlines, his mind going blank when he tries to focus on a complex form. His colleagues have noticed the change. They say he seems "distracted," "jumpy." They do not know the truth.

He has not told anyone the full story. Not his ex-wife, not his adult daughter. He is ashamed. He is a professional man, a man who solves problems with logic and numbers. He cannot reconcile the image of himself, a man in a pressed shirt and tie, with the memory of being pinned to the ground like a criminal. He feels a deep, corrosive guilt, as if he must have done something to provoke it, even though he knows, intellectually, that he did not.

He sits in the office now, his eyes fixed on a spot on the wall. He says he is here because his doctor said his blood pressure is dangerously high. He does not say he is here because he is tired of the constant fear, the feeling of being trapped in his own life. He does not say he is here because he cannot remember the last time he felt safe. He simply says, "I need to get this under control." The words are precise, clinical, a perfect summary of a man trying to manage a catastrophe with the only tools he has left.
